name: Slave
catalog_citation: Rice, Keren. 1989. A Grammar of Slave. (Mouton Grammar Library 5.) Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter. [as quoted in the StressTyp2 entry for this language]
catalog_quote: Stress is not a distinctive feature in Slave. In the Hare dialect, there are stress-like properties which are predictable. What might be called stress generally falls on the vowel immediately preceding the stem vowel of a noun. A stressed vowel is generally acoustically more intense than an unstressed vowel, and intensity is in fact the primary phonetic correlate of stress. In prefixes in all dialects, a high tone may fall on a vowel with lexical high tone. That vowel then has extra stress, or is more intense. In the perfective, the first and third person singular forms differ only by tone placement. Where the high tone falls on a vowel already bearing a hight tone, as in the first person singular perfective form, this vowel retains its tone and receives prominent stress Rice (1989:46)

audit.recode_to: morphological (stem-controlled prominence): stem syllable stressed in nouns and, in all dialects but Hare, in verbs; Hare verbs stress the pre-stem syllable; lexical high tone independent of stress; stress non-contrastive, correlate intensity. At minimum: replace the corrupted quote/the domain quotation with the true p. 46 wording ('..immediately preceding the stem of a verb and on the stem vowel of a noun'), fix the primary-stress rule accordingly, and cite Rice & Hargus 2005:35 / Rice 2005 as the deciding sources. If house convention files every tone language with non-contrastive stress under 'tonal', keep kind but the the primary-stress rule/quote fix is still mandatory.

sources.quote: '... Rice this volume (for Slave non-verbal elements and verbs in most dialects) note that the stem is stressed in these languages. However, for verbs in the Hare dialect of Slave, stress falls on the pre-stem syllable, making Hare different from the other Slave dialects where the stem is stressed regardless of category. Morphology thus plays a major role in determining the placement of stress. However, phonological factors, such as syllable weight and position within the word, enter in as well. In ...' (the last sentence is about the family survey, not specifically Slave).
sources.note: Family-wide prosody survey; p. 35 (snippet downloaded now) states the stem is stressed in Slave, pre-stem in Hare verbs, 'morphology thus plays a major role in determining the placement of stress' -- full pages 33-36 needed for the exact scope and the syllable-weight remark.
